design.control_model: The parent calls operation steps directly. Comparison reads fixed records and returns. Continuation first obtains a reuse plan, then rechecks its relevant inputs before creating a new attempt. If those inputs changed, it repeats the check or reports that the plan is outdated. The parent controller starts s08 work and accepts results only for the active attempt. It saves each accepted unit with progress before accepting further progress. Import checks all required data before requesting publication. No event queue, second scheduler, or separate service is added.

design.failure_isolation: Preparation failures leave saved records unchanged. A failed unit save stops the affected attempt while retaining earlier accepted units. Cancellation prevents late output from being accepted. A failed import leaves its temporary data unpublished. Failed exports do not change their source records. After a crash, the parent uses saved progress to prepare another continuation. These rules protect completed work but do not contain a failure of the shared process or disk.

value_json.summary: I agree with the supplied assessment. Service-oriented architecture means offering reusable operations to other, separately run systems, with clear inputs, results, owners and error rules. AnaxiGraph already reaches its operations through a command line, a web API and MCP. MCP is a way for coding agents to call tools over a network connection. All three routes share one database, one history service and one set of service objects inside a single program. The payload has no example of an outside system that needs these operations under its own release schedule or owner. value_json.summary: The supplied assessment holds up. A proxy is an object that takes the same calls as another object and controls access to it, for example by checking permission, loading the object late, or saving results. The supplied code shows objects that pass calls along, but none that controls access. _CountingAnalyzer counts calls and then passes them on, so it is closer to a decorator, which is a wrapper that adds extra work around a call. SemanticEngine sends calls on to several services, which is a different design. AnaxiIndex extends a parent class instead of wrapping another object. The best possible place for a proxy, the three semantic providers, is correctly described as conditional. Keeping the current design is well supported, and the scores match the evidence.

issues.explanation: The claim update runs inside database.transaction(). If that transaction takes the database write lock, a status check inside it acts more like a safety backstop than a true optimistic check. Optimistic concurrency means no lock is held: the writer checks a version number at save time instead. Most stale-write protection comes from the lease, meaning the worker id, token hash and expiry time recorded with each claim. That is closer to a lease with an ownership token than to version-based optimistic concurrency.

value_json.summary: The assessment picks the right first place: the three-try loop in graph_read. But it misses three things already in the code that matter for any retry design. The semantic job queue already has a "retry" job state. The fresh-eyes start code says on purpose that the CLI does not retry a request that was turned away for being too busy. The CLI also already waits through a 30-second busy window. Without these, the provider-retry idea could stack a second layer of retries on top of the first. Confidence is also set too high, because only 8 of 845 files have detailed descriptions and no failure types were supplied. The corrected version keeps the recommendation to improve the graph_read loop and adds these facts.
